quickReference.title: Water Properties & Macromolecule Structure
quickReference.purpose: Anchors how hydrogen bonding, polymer assembly, and directional monomer linkages dictate biological structure and function on AP Biology items.
checklist: Identify whether the prompt focuses on polar water interactions or covalent linkages inside a specific macromolecule class.
Check polymer directionality (N-terminus to C-terminus for polypeptides; 5' to 3' for nucleic acids) before interpreting structural diagrams.
Trace how a change in R-group polarity, charge, or pH alters tertiary folding rather than primary amino acid sequence.
formulas: Water properties from H-bonding: cohesion (transpiration pull), adhesion, high specific heat, evaporative cooling, and lower solid density (ice floats).
Dehydration synthesis removes H2O to join monomers (glycosidic, ester, peptide, phosphodiester bonds); hydrolysis consumes H2O to cleave polymers.
Protein hierarchy: primary (peptide bonds), secondary (backbone H-bonds: alpha-helices/beta-sheets), tertiary (R-group interactions), quaternary (multi-subunit).
Nucleic acids: antiparallel DNA strands pair A-T (2 H-bonds) and G-C (3 H-bonds); RNA uses ribose, uracil, and typically folds single-stranded.
decisionRules: When you see a point mutation replacing a hydrophilic charged R-group with a nonpolar R-group → predict disrupted surface folding or altered active-site binding.
When you see a double-stranded DNA sample with a higher G-C percentage → choose a higher melting temperature due to more hydrogen bonds per base pair.
When you see a lipid with cis double bonds in its hydrocarbon tails → interpret kinks that prevent tight packing and increase membrane fluidity.
When you see a coastal climate moderating temperature swings or organisms cooling via sweating → attribute the effect to hydrogen bonds requiring high heat energy to break.
cautions: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules or DNA base pairs are intermolecular/noncovalent attractions, not covalent bonds within a single water molecule.
Denaturation unfolds secondary, tertiary, and quaternary protein structure by disrupting weak R-group/backbone interactions, leaving primary peptide bonds intact.
Lipids are hydrophobic macromolecules assembled from glycerol and fatty acids (or steroid rings), not true repeating-monomer polymers.

quickReference.title: Compartmentalization, Transport & Water Potential
quickReference.purpose: Links organelle trafficking, surface-area-to-volume limits, membrane permeability, and quantitative water potential calculations.
checklist: Determine whether solute movement goes down its electrochemical gradient (passive) or against it using ATP or a coupled gradient (active).
Check if solutes are permeable or impermeable to the membrane before predicting net osmotic water movement.
Verify temperature is converted to Kelvin (K = °C + 273) and ionization constant i matches electrolyte dissociation before solving water potential.
formulas: Surface-area-to-volume ratios: cube SA/V = 6/s and sphere SA/V = 3/r; smaller cells or folded membranes maximize exchange efficiency.
Water potential: Ψ = Ψp + Ψs, where solute potential Ψs = −iCRT with R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K) and water always flows from higher Ψ to lower Ψ.
Endomembrane export pathway: rough ER ribosome synthesis → transport vesicle → cis-to-trans Golgi modification → secretory vesicle exocytosis.
Endosymbiotic evidence for mitochondria and chloroplasts: double membranes, circular DNA, independent binary-like division, and bacterial-type ribosomes.
decisionRules: When you see a plant cell placed in a solution with a more negative Ψ than the cell interior → predict net water efflux, loss of turgor pressure, and plasmolysis.
When you see small nonpolar molecules (O2, CO2, steroid hormones) crossing a phospholipid bilayer → choose simple diffusion without transport proteins.
When you see ions or polar molecules moving down their gradient across a hydrophobic bilayer core → choose facilitated diffusion via channel or carrier proteins.
When you see a cell line with extensive rough ER and Golgi stacks → interpret specialization for synthesizing and secreting proteins.
cautions: Adding solute always makes solute potential Ψs more negative; pure water in an open beaker has Ψp = 0 and Ψs = 0.
Do not confuse hypertonic with high water potential: a hypertonic solution has higher solute concentration and therefore lower (more negative) water potential.
Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles, but they still possess a plasma membrane, cytosol, circular DNA, and ribosomes.

quickReference.title: Enzymes, Photosynthesis & Cellular Respiration
quickReference.purpose: Organizes enzyme catalysis kinetics alongside the compartmentalized inputs, outputs, and proton-gradient coupling of photosynthesis and respiration.
checklist: Separate reaction rate changes caused by substrate/inhibitor concentration from structural enzyme denaturation caused by extreme heat or pH.
Pinpoint the exact sub-organelle compartment (cytosol, mitochondrial matrix, cristae, thylakoid membrane, or stroma) where each energetic step occurs.
Track electron carriers (NADH, FADH2, NADPH) to distinguish ATP-generating chemiosmosis from carbon-fixing or substrate-level steps.
formulas: Enzyme catalysis: lowers activation energy (Ea) by stabilizing the transition state without altering overall ΔG of reactants and products.
Photosynthesis: thylakoid light reactions split H2O to produce O2, ATP, and NADPH; stroma Calvin cycle uses ATP, NADPH, and Rubisco to fix CO2 into G3P.
Aerobic respiration: glycolysis (cytosol) → pyruvate oxidation & citric acid cycle (matrix) → ETC + chemiosmosis across inner mitochondrial membrane (O2 → H2O).
Fermentation (lactic acid or alcoholic): occurs anaerobically in cytosol solely to oxidize NADH back to NAD+ so glycolysis can continue producing 2 net ATP.
decisionRules: When you see reaction rate restored to maximum Vmax by flooding the assay with excess substrate → identify competitive inhibition at the active site.
When you see a protonophore making the inner mitochondrial or thylakoid membrane leaky to H+ → predict collapsed proton motive force, halted ATP synthase output, and continued electron flow as heat.
When you see leaves placed in darkness after light exposure → predict light reactions stop immediately and the Calvin cycle soon stalls once ATP and NADPH run out.
When you see O2 removed from facultative anaerobes → predict the mitochondrial ETC backs up and cells switch to fermentation to regenerate NAD+.
cautions: Enzymes never make an endergonic reaction exergonic; they speed approach to equilibrium without changing ΔG.
Plants perform both photosynthesis and cellular respiration continuously (respiration runs in light and dark alike).
Fermentation produces zero additional ATP beyond glycolysis; its metabolic role is regenerating the NAD+ pool.

quickReference.title: Signal Transduction, Feedback & Cell Cycle Control
quickReference.purpose: Connects ligand-receptor specificity, second-messenger amplification, homeostatic feedback loops, and checkpoint regulation of mitosis.
checklist: Check whether the signaling ligand is hydrophilic (binds plasma-membrane receptor) or hydrophobic/steroid (crosses membrane to intracellular receptor).
Trace upstream vs. downstream components in a transduction pathway to predict which step still activates if a mutation locks one protein ON or OFF.
Distinguish interphase preparation (G1, S, G2) from mitotic nuclear division (PMAT) and cytokinesis before counting DNA content or chromatids.
formulas: Signal transduction stages: reception (ligand-receptor conformational change) → transduction (phosphorylation cascade, cAMP/Ca2+ second messengers) → cellular response.
Signaling range: direct contact (gap junctions, plasmodesmata, immune APCs), local (paracrine/synaptic), and long-distance (endocrine hormones in bloodstream).

Feedback loops: negative feedback opposes deviations to restore a set point (insulin/glucagon blood glucose); positive feedback amplifies a process to completion (oxytocin in labor, ethylene fruit ripening).
Cell cycle control: G1, G2, and M (spindle) checkpoints governed by oscillating cyclins binding constant CDKs; DNA damage triggers p53 arrest or apoptosis.
decisionRules: When you see two different target cell types exposed to the same hormone producing distinct responses → attribute the difference to distinct receptor isoforms or intracellular relay proteins.
When you see a drug blocking a downstream kinase while the receptor still binds its ligand → predict signal amplification halts downstream of the blocked kinase.
When you see loss-of-function mutations in both alleles of a tumor suppressor gene (like p53) or gain-of-function in a proto-oncogene → predict checkpoint bypass and uncontrolled proliferation.
When you see rising product concentration inhibiting an early pathway step to stabilize an internal variable → classify the mechanism as negative feedback.
cautions: A ligand does not enter the cell during GPCR or RTK signaling; only conformational information is relayed across the membrane.
DNA replication occurs during S phase of interphase, not during prophase or metaphase of mitosis.
Positive feedback is not inherently harmful or "good"; it simply amplifies change away from baseline until a terminating event occurs.

quickReference.title: Meiosis, Pedigrees & Chi-Square Genetics
quickReference.purpose: Guides chromosome segregation accounting, inheritance-pattern deduction, and statistical hypothesis testing with chi-square distributions.
checklist: Identify whether a cross tests independent assortment, sex linkage, autosomal linkage, or non-nuclear maternal inheritance before calculating expected ratios.
Count degrees of freedom as phenotypic categories minus one (df = n − 1) and use the p = 0.05 row unless the prompt specifies another alpha level.
Verify whether pedigree traits skip generations (recessive) or affect fathers-to-all-daughters (X-linked dominant) versus carrier mothers-to-sons (X-linked recessive).
formulas: Meiosis variation mechanisms: prophase I crossing over (chiasmata), metaphase I independent assortment (2^n combinations), and random fertilization.
Probability laws: multiplication rule P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events; addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) for mutually exclusive outcomes.
Chi-square goodness-of-fit: χ² = Σ((O − E)² / E), df = n − 1; reject the null hypothesis when calculated χ² exceeds the critical value at p = 0.05.
Gene linkage: recombination frequency = (recombinant offspring / total offspring) × 100%; frequencies below 50% indicate genes linked on the same chromosome.
decisionRules: When you see a dihybrid testcross yielding far more parental phenotypes than recombinant phenotypes → conclude the two loci are physically linked on the same chromosome.
When you see every offspring of an affected mother inherit a trait regardless of the father's phenotype → identify mitochondrial or chloroplast (extranuclear) inheritance.
When you see calculated χ² smaller than the p = 0.05 critical value → fail to reject the null hypothesis and conclude deviations are consistent with random chance.
When you see genetically identical plants showing different flower colors in acidic vs. alkaline soil → identify phenotypic plasticity driven by environmental interaction.
cautions: Never say a low chi-square value "proves" the null hypothesis; AP rubrics require "fail to reject the null hypothesis."
Homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I (halving ploidy 2n → n), whereas sister chromatids separate in anaphase II.
Nondisjunction in meiosis I produces all four gametes with abnormal chromosome numbers, whereas nondisjunction in meiosis II leaves half the gametes normal.

quickReference.title: DNA Replication, Transcription, Operons & Biotech
quickReference.purpose: Synthesizes nucleic acid polarity rules, prokaryotic vs. eukaryotic gene regulation, mutation effects, and core molecular biotechnology assays.
checklist: Confirm strand labels (3'→5' template vs. 5'→3' coding/mRNA) before transcribing codons or reading the genetic code table.
Check whether the organism is prokaryotic (coupled transcription-translation, operons, no introns) or eukaryotic (nuclear mRNA processing, enhancers, chromatin remodeling).
Examine how a single nucleotide insertion or deletion shifts the downstream reading frame relative to a base substitution.
formulas: Semiconservative DNA replication: helicase unwinds, topoisomerase relieves supercoiling, primase lays RNA primer, DNA polymerase III extends 5'→3' (leading continuous; lagging Okazaki fragments), ligase seals nicks.
Eukaryotic mRNA processing: 5' GTP cap, 3' poly-A tail, and spliceosome intron removal; alternative splicing generates distinct protein isoforms from one gene.
Prokaryotic operons: lac operon (inducible: allolactose inactivates repressor; high cAMP-CAP boosts transcription when glucose is low); trp operon (repressible: tryptophan activates repressor).
Chromatin epigenetics: histone acetylation loosens nucleosomes to increase transcription; DNA/histone methylation typically condenses chromatin and silences expression.
decisionRules: When you see DNA fragments separated on an agarose gel → read smaller fragments closer to the positive (anode) end because negatively charged DNA migrates faster when shorter.
When you see a bacterial transformation plate with LB + ampicillin + arabinose showing glowing colonies → confirm bacteria took up the plasmid carrying both ampR and an inducible reporter gene.
When you see a base substitution changing a sense codon into UAA, UAG, or UGA → classify it as a nonsense mutation producing a truncated, usually nonfunctional polypeptide.
When you see a eukaryotic liver cell and neuron expressing different proteins despite identical genomes → explain differential expression via cell-specific transcription factors binding enhancers.
cautions: DNA and RNA polymerases ALWAYS synthesize new nucleic acid strands in the 5'→3' direction by reading the template strand 3'→5'.
Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to make cDNA from an RNA template, which does not violate the broader flow of genetic information once integrated into host DNA.
Introns are spliced out of eukaryotic pre-mRNA and are not translated; exons are the retained sequences expressed in mature mRNA.

quickReference.title: Evolutionary Mechanisms, Hardy-Weinberg & Phylogenies
quickReference.purpose: Anchors quantitative allele-frequency equilibrium checks, modes of selection and speciation, and rigorous phylogenetic tree reading.
checklist: Determine whether given percentages represent genotype frequencies (q², 2pq, p²) or allele frequencies (p, q) before solving Hardy-Weinberg problems.
Check if a trait reflects shared ancestry (homologous/synapomorphy) or independent adaptation to similar environments (convergent/analogous).
Verify evolutionary statements act on populations over generations rather than individuals intentionally adapting during their lifetimes.
formulas: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium: p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1; requires large population, random mating, no mutation, no gene flow, and no natural selection.

Evolutionary drivers: natural selection (adaptive), genetic drift (random bottleneck/founder effects strongest in small populations), gene flow (homogenizes populations), and mutation (source of new alleles).

Speciation modes: allopatric (geographic barrier isolates gene pools) vs. sympatric (polyploidy, habitat/behavioral isolation without physical barrier), maintained by prezygotic or postzygotic barriers.
Phylogenetics: nodes represent most recent common ancestors; rotating branches around a node leaves evolutionary relationships unchanged; parsimony favors the fewest evolutionary events.
decisionRules: When you see 16% of a population displaying a recessive phenotype in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium → set q² = 0.16, take q = 0.4, find p = 0.6, and compute heterozygote frequency 2pq = 0.48.
When you see two taxa sharing the most recent node on a cladogram → identify them as sister taxa regardless of visual left-to-right tip spacing.
When you see pesticide resistance emerging rapidly after spraying → explain that pre-existing resistant variants survived and reproduced more, shifting allele frequencies.
When you see an allele rapidly fixed or lost following a hurricane that leaves only 15 survivors → attribute the shift to a population bottleneck (genetic drift), not selection.
cautions: Never take the square root of the dominant phenotype frequency (p² + 2pq) to find p; always start from the homozygous recessive frequency q².
Antibiotics and pesticides do not cause targeted resistance mutations; random mutations arise prior to selection.
Cladogram branch tip proximity does not measure relatedness; always trace back to the most recent shared internal node.

quickReference.title: Population Growth, Energy Flow & Community Dynamics
quickReference.purpose: Links differential population models, diversity indices, trophic energy budgets, and ecological disruption cascades.
checklist: Check whether population data show unrestricted exponential acceleration or a plateau approaching carrying capacity K.
Distinguish primary productivity terms (GPP, NPP, cellular respiration R) and ensure energy units match across trophic levels.
Trace both direct predation and indirect trophic cascade ripples across food webs before predicting species abundance shifts.
formulas: Exponential growth: dN/dt = rmax·N (J-curve with abundant resources); Logistic growth: dN/dt = rmax·N·((K − N)/K) (S-curve, fastest growth at N = K/2).
Simpson's Diversity Index: SDI = 1 − Σ(n/N)², ranging from 0 to 1; higher values signify greater species richness and evenness and stronger ecosystem resilience.
Primary productivity & trophic transfer: NPP = GPP − R; roughly 10% of assimilated energy transfers to the next trophic level while ~90% is lost as metabolic heat and waste.
Community structure: competitive exclusion prevents identical-niche coexistence; resource partitioning enables coexistence; keystone species exert disproportionate control over biodiversity.
decisionRules: When you see a population size N exceed carrying capacity K → predict dN/dt turns negative and population declines due to density-dependent resource limits.
When you see removal of a top predator followed by herbivore explosion and kelp/plant collapse → identify a top-down trophic cascade indicating a keystone predator.
When you see a non-native species expanding exponentially in a new habitat → attribute its success to release from native predators, pathogens, and competitors.
When you see an animal sacrificing personal reproduction to help siblings raise offspring → explain the behavior via kin selection and inclusive fitness.
cautions: Energy flows one-way through ecosystems and dissipates as heat, whereas matter (carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, water) recycles continuously.
In logistic growth, per-capita growth rate decreases continuously as N approaches K, while total population growth rate dN/dt peaks at N = K/2.
A species with the largest biomass (foundation species/dominant producer) is not automatically a keystone species, whose impact is disproportionate to its low abundance.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Correlation vs. Biological Mechanism
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners mistake a co-occurring trend in a data table or graph for a proven causal cellular or physiological pathway, skipping the intermediate molecular step that links stimulus to response.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Trace the explicit molecular chain from signal or perturbation → intermediate molecule or pathway step → measured biological outcome before accepting any causal claim.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Teleological and Need-Driven Evolution
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners select distractors claiming organisms mutate, adapt, or develop traits in order to survive an environmental change, rather than recognizing pre-existing heritable variation filtered by differential reproductive success.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Rewrite every evolutionary explanation in three strict steps: pre-existing random variation → selective pressure → higher reproductive fitness increasing allele frequency across generations.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Water Potential and Osmosis Sign Reversal
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners drop the negative sign in solute potential (Ψs = −iCRT), omit turgor pressure potential (Ψp), or reverse net osmotic flow by moving water toward higher solute potential instead of from higher total Ψ to lower total Ψ.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Compute Ψ = Ψp + Ψs for both compartments with explicit signs, place both values on a signed number line, and draw the osmosis arrow strictly from the more positive Ψ → more negative Ψ.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Gene Regulation and Operon Logic Inversion
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners invert inducible (lac) and repressible (trp) operon switches, confuse corepressors with inducers, or conflate cis-acting promoter/operator mutations with trans-acting repressor protein mutations.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Build a 2-state operon truth table mapping effector presence → repressor conformation → operator occupancy → RNA polymerase transcription rate before reading the answer choices.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Experimental Control and Confounding Variable Blindness
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners misclassify negative vs. positive controls, treat overlapping ±2 SE error bars as statistically distinct outcomes, or attribute treatment differences to the wrong independent variable when two conditions vary simultaneously.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Audit the experimental design by naming the single manipulated independent variable, the matched negative control baseline, and whether ±2 SE error bars overlap before endorsing any data conclusion.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Population vs. Individual Scale Conflation
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners apply single-organism physiology, gamete segregation, or individual acclimation directly to population-level metrics such as allele frequencies (p and q), genetic drift, or logistic carrying capacity (K).
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Tag the unit of analysis first (single cell, individual organism, or breeding population) and match the quantitative tool (Punnett ratio vs. Hardy-Weinberg p² + 2pq + q² = 1 vs. dN/dt) strictly to that scale.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Separating Observed Biological Trends from Proven Cellular Mechanisms
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You selected an option asserting that variable X directly activates or inhibits pathway Y even though the graph only reports an association without blocking or isolating an intermediate step.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: What specific molecular intermediate or experimental perturbation would be required to prove direct causation rather than a shared upstream trigger?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Inspect the stimulus figure or table and circle the exact measured variables on both axes, flagging any answer choice that inserts an unmeasured enzyme, receptor, or direct causal verb.
stages.requiredOutput: A two-column note listing what the graph directly measures versus the unproven causal step claimed by the distractor.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Map the cellular pathway using a three-node chain (input signal → tested intermediate → measured readout) and note where an alternative shared factor could produce the same correlation.
stages.requiredOutput: A completed three-node mechanism diagram plus one plausible third biological factor that could explain the observed association.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Compare two AP Biology energetics or signal-transduction data sets: one with an inhibitor knockout and one purely observational, labeling which supports a mechanistic claim.
stages.requiredOutput: A side-by-side justification showing why the inhibitor trial supports causation while the observational dataset supports only association.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-attempt the missed item and solve a new cell-communication or enzyme-kinetics graph item by disqualifying every distractor that overstates mechanism beyond the experimental evidence.
stages.requiredOutput: Correct selection on both items accompanied by a one-sentence evidence check tying the winning choice to the exact experimental manipulation.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Replacing Need-Based Adaptation Language with Selection Mechanics
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You chose an answer containing goal-directed phrasing such as "mutated to resist", "adapted so it could survive", or "developed traits because the habitat changed".
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Did the favorable allele appear after the selective pressure as a purposeful response, or did it already exist randomly before selection shifted survival and reproduction?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Underline every teleological trigger phrase ("in order to", "needed to", "tried to", "became resistant to survive") across the answer choices of the missed natural-selection item.
stages.requiredOutput: A marked list of goal-directed distractor phrases and why each violates random mutation and non-random selection.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Rebuild the evolutionary explanation using the AP Bio 4-part frame: pre-existing variation → selective agent → differential reproductive success → shift in population allele frequency.
stages.requiredOutput: A four-clause non-teleological explanation of the scenario that never attributes intent or need to organisms or mutations.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Rewrite two classic AP evolution prompts (antibiotic resistance in bacteria and pesticide resistance in insects) from teleological statements into mechanistic selection statements.
stages.requiredOutput: Two corrected mechanistic paragraphs specifying the timing of mutation relative to exposure and the fitness metric (offspring count).

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-solve the missed Unit 7 item and one novel speciation or genetic-drift item, eliminating any distractor that describes individuals evolving during a single lifetime.
stages.requiredOutput: Verified correct responses on both items with explicit identification of the selective pressure and population-level allele shift.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Water Potential and Osmosis Sign Reversal
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Locking Down Water Potential Signs and Net Osmosis Direction
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You calculated a positive solute potential, treated a more negative Ψ value as "larger", or predicted water moving out of a hypotonic bath into a higher-Ψ cell.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: After computing Ψ = Ψp + (−iCRT) for both the cell and the surrounding solution, which numerical value sits further to the right on the number line?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Audit your calculation from the missed cell-transport item to pinpoint whether the error came from dropping the minus sign in −iCRT, misreading ionization constant i (sucrose i = 1 vs. NaCl i = 2), or comparing absolute values instead of signed numbers.
stages.requiredOutput: An error diagnosis tagging the exact sign, constant, or direction reversal in the original calculation.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Plot both Ψ_cell and Ψ_solution on a horizontal number line from −15 bar to +5 bar and draw the net water-movement arrow strictly from right (higher Ψ) → left (lower Ψ).
stages.requiredOutput: A labeled signed calculation for both compartments, the number-line placement, and the resulting tonicity and mass-change prediction.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Solve two paired osmosis drills: one open-beaker plant cell (Ψp = 0 in beaker, positive Ψp in turgid cell) and one sucrose-vs-NaCl comparison at equal molarity.
stages.requiredOutput: Step-by-step Ψs, Ψp, and total Ψ values for both drills showing why 0.2 M NaCl has twice the magnitude of Ψs compared with 0.2 M sucrose.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-attempt the original Unit 2 transport item and a fresh dialysis-tubing or potato-core percent-mass-change graph item using the signed number-line check.
stages.requiredOutput: Accurate answers on both items plus a brief explanation of the zero-percent-mass-change x-intercept (isotonic molarity).

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Gene Regulation and Operon Logic Inversion
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Tracing Inducible vs. Repressible Operon and Mutation Logic
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You predicted transcription turns ON when tryptophan binds the trp repressor, or assumed a mutated operator still allows a normal repressor protein to block RNA polymerase.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: In this operon, is the default repressor active or inactive without its small-molecule effector, and does the mutation break DNA binding at the operator or effector binding on the repressor?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Classify the operon in the prompt as inducible (catabolic, default OFF, such as lac) or repressible (anabolic, default ON, such as trp) and mark where your original prediction flipped the switch.
stages.requiredOutput: A clear label of operon class, default transcriptional state, and the exact polarity flip in your previous answer.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Construct a 4-row state table (effector absent/present × wild-type/mutant) tracking repressor shape → operator binding → RNA polymerase access → mRNA output.
stages.requiredOutput: A completed 4-row operon logic table distinguishing loss of operator affinity (constitutive ON) from loss of inducer affinity (constitutive OFF).

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Predict transcription outcomes for three classic AP Bio mutations: a deleted promoter, a mutated lac operator that cannot bind repressor, and a lac repressor unable to bind allolactose.
stages.requiredOutput: Three concise predictions specifying whether structural enzymes are never made or continuously made regardless of lactose presence.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-solve the missed Unit 6 item and transfer the regulatory-switch checklist to a eukaryotic transcription-factor or epigenetic chromatin-remodeling question.
stages.requiredOutput: Correct selections on both items with a note explaining how DNA accessibility governs RNA polymerase initiation in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Experimental Control and Confounding Variable Blindness
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Auditing Controls, Confounders, and ±2 SE Error Bars
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You claimed two treatment means were significantly different despite overlapping ±2 SE error bars, or picked a control group that changed more than one variable at once.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Which single variable differs between the experimental and control treatments, and do the ±2 SE bars separate cleanly enough to reject the null hypothesis?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Inspect the experimental setup and bar/line graph from the missed item, highlighting any secondary condition (pH, temperature, solvent, or buffer) not held constant and checking error-bar overlap.
stages.requiredOutput: An audit listing the intended independent variable, any uncontrolled confounder, and a yes/no check on ±2 SE error-bar overlap.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Specify what a proper negative control (baseline without active treatment) and positive control (known working response) must contain so only one factor varies.
stages.requiredOutput: A two-line control specification stating the exact composition and expected baseline reading for both negative and positive controls.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Evaluate two enzyme-assay scenarios: one where boiled enzyme serves as a negative control and one where two treatments have overlapping 95% CI bars despite different sample means.
stages.requiredOutput: Written verdicts explaining why boiled enzyme isolates catalytic activity and why overlapping ±2 SE bars prevent claiming a statistically significant difference.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-attempt the missed AP Biology lab-design item and solve a second unfamiliar data-analysis prompt using the single-variable and error-bar checklist.
stages.requiredOutput: Correct choices on both items supported by explicit reference to the control baseline and error-bar separation.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Matching Biological Reasoning to Individual vs. Population Scale
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You used an individual Punnett-square genotype ratio to answer a population allele-frequency question, or claimed an individual organism evolves or shifts carrying capacity on its own.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Is the prompt asking about one organism and its offspring, or about allele frequencies and density-dependent growth across an entire interbreeding population?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Underline the biological unit named in the stem ("individual", "gamete", "offspring", "population", "gene pool", or "community") and compare it against the scale assumed by your missed answer.
stages.requiredOutput: A brief mismatch note stating the scale required by the prompt versus the scale used in the distractor.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Pair each biological scale with its governing math: individual cross → Punnett probability; population genetics → q² (homozygous recessive frequency) → q → p = 1 − q → 2pq; ecology → dN/dt = r_max N (K − N)/K.
stages.requiredOutput: A scale-to-tool reference card showing why dominant phenotype frequency equals p² + 2pq rather than p alone.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Work two contrasting items: a Hardy-Weinberg problem starting from 16% recessive phenotype (q² = 0.16 → q = 0.4 → 2pq = 0.48) and a logistic growth problem explaining why per-capita growth slows as N approaches K.
stages.requiredOutput: Exact carrier-frequency calculation and a density-dependent explanation of why population growth rate peaks near K/2 rather than at K.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-solve the original Unit 5 or Unit 8 item and complete one cross-unit transfer item linking genetic drift or bottleneck effects to population-level heterozygosity.
stages.requiredOutput: Correct solutions on both items with an explicit scale verification line before each final choice.
